hook.text: Massive jaw muscles, huge flat teeth, a bony skull crest — built to chew tough plants all day long.

buildup.text: Robust australopithecines (Paranthropus) had powerful chewing muscles anchored to a sagittal crest on the skull.

discovery.text: They specialized in hard, fibrous foods — seeds, roots, and tough plants that other hominins couldn't process.

twist.text: Specialization was their downfall. When climates shifted and food sources changed, they couldn't adapt and went extinct.

climax.text: Paranthropus shows that evolution has no guaranteed winners. Specialization is a gamble against future change.

punchline.text: The specialists lost; the generalists survived.

quiz.question: Why did robust australopithecines go extinct?
options: Their dietary specialization failed when climates changed

details.summary: Robust australopithecines (Paranthropus) were heavily built hominins with massive jaws, large molars, and bony skull crests for anchoring powerful chewing muscles. They specialized in eating tough, fibrous plant foods and coexisted with early Homo before going extinct around 1 million years ago.
details.whyItMatters: Paranthropus shows that human evolution was not a single line toward us. A separate lineage of hominins evolved specialized adaptations for millions of years before going extinct.
takeaways: Robust australopithecines had massive jaws and specialized chewing anatomy
They coexisted with early Homo for over a million years
Their extinction shows human survival was contingent, not inevitable

faq.question: Why did the robust australopithecines go extinct?
faq.answer: Their dietary specialization may have made them vulnerable when environments changed. While early Homo adapted through tool use and dietary flexibility, Paranthropus was committed to tough plant foods. Climate change likely reduced their food sources while generalist competitors thrived.

faq.question: How many species of Paranthropus existed?
faq.answer: Three species are widely recognized: Paranthropus aethiopicus, Paranthropus boisei, and Paranthropus robustus. They lived in eastern and southern Africa between about 2.7 and 1 million years ago, overlapping in time and sometimes in place with early members of the genus Homo.
